opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think complementarity is really one of the central parameters in the whole picture, because it determines how much you get out of automating only part of the economy before you've automated all of it.

The way to think about it is this: suppose AI systems can do, say, 30% of the tasks in the economy, and they can do them extremely cheaply and at enormous scale. If tasks were highly substitutable with one another, you'd expect output to just explode, because you could pour huge amounts of AI labor into those 30% of tasks and that would substitute for everything else. But in reality, the economy looks a lot more like a system with strong complementarity. You need many different inputs, and if one of them is scarce, it becomes a bottleneck. So if you've automated 30% of tasks, the remaining 70% that still require human labor end up constraining how much output you can actually get. The automated tasks become very cheap, their share of the value in the economy shrinks, and the human-performed tasks become where all the value and the constraints sit. That's a kind of Baumol effect.

In GATE, this matters for timelines in a couple of ways. First, it shapes how much economic growth you get from partial automation, and that feeds back into how much investment flows into compute and AI development. If complementarity is strong, partial automation gives you relatively modest gains until you get close to full automation, and then you get a very sharp acceleration at the end. If complementarity is weak, you get a more gradual, earlier speedup. So it really affects the shape of the trajectory, whether you see something like a smooth ramp or a period where things look fairly normal and then change abruptly.

Second, it affects what you should infer from current evidence. If someone says, "AI can already do a lot of impressive things, so why don't we see it in GDP statistics?", strong complementarity is part of the answer. You wouldn't necessarily expect large macroeconomic effects even if AI is quite capable at a decent fraction of tasks, because the bottlenecks dominate. That means the absence of big growth effects today isn't strong evidence that transformative AI is far away.

And my own view is that the evidence we have, from historical episodes of automation and from how economies respond to shocks, suggests complementarity is quite strong. So in the model, I'd expect a world where growth effects are relatively muted for a while, and then once you get to automating the bulk of tasks, especially the ones that are currently bottlenecks, things can accelerate very dramatically. That's quite different from the picture people sometimes have where every incremental capability gain translates straightforwardly into proportional economic gains.

r001.rationale: It explains that complementarity determines how much output rises before all tasks are automated, with remaining human-performed tasks acting as bottlenecks.

r002.rationale: It states that growth from partial automation feeds back into investment in compute and AI development.

r003.rationale: It connects automation-driven growth to investment and discusses timeline trajectories, but does not clearly state that reinvesting those gains can shorten AI timelines.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the degree of complementarity is probably the single most important parameter in the model, and the reason is that it governs how much the economy can actually benefit from automating only part of what it does.

The way to think about it is: production requires a bunch of different tasks, and the question is how substitutable those tasks are for one another. If they're highly substitutable, then automating, say, half the tasks and making them a thousand times cheaper gives you something close to a thousandfold increase in output, because you can just lean on the cheap stuff and barely need the rest. But if the tasks are strongly complementary, then output is bottlenecked by whichever tasks you haven't automated yet. You can make the automated half essentially free and it won't matter much, because you still need the humans doing the other half, and there are only so many of them and they only work so fast. That's the Baumol effect, basically. The sectors that don't get automated eat up a growing share of spending and the aggregate growth rate stays pinned to the slowest-moving part.

So in GATE, this shows up in a couple of ways. One is how much economic acceleration you get before full automation. With low complementarity, you get a lot of growth while you're still at, say, 50 or 80 percent of tasks automated, and that growth feeds back into more compute investment, more R&D, faster progress. With high complementarity, you get almost nothing until you're very close to 100 percent, and then everything happens at once. The second thing is the feedback loop itself. If AI is a complement to human researchers rather than a substitute, then AI doing more and more of the R&D work doesn't speed things up that much, because the remaining human steps are still the binding constraint. If it's a substitute, you get the full software-feedback-loop story where progress compounds.

And the honest answer is that we don't know this parameter very well. Historical estimates from the elasticity of substitution literature tend to suggest things are fairly complementary, with elasticities below one, and that's part of why historical automation hasn't produced explosive growth. But those estimates come from a regime where the automated and non-automated tasks were pretty different in kind, and it's not obvious they transfer to a world where AI can do cognitive work generally. That's why we treat it as something you should vary across a range rather than pick a point estimate, and the timelines you get out depend heavily on where in that range you land.

r001.rationale: The response explains that substitutability determines how much output can rise when only part of the tasks are automated, while complementarity makes remaining tasks bottlenecks.

r002.rationale: It says growth from partial automation feeds into more compute investment and R&D.

r003.rationale: It connects reinvestment of that growth to faster progress, communicating that automation-driven gains can accelerate AI development and shorten timelines.

astra-6.text:
The degree of complementarity matters because it determines how much progress you can get by automating some parts of production while other parts remain difficult to automate. If different tasks are strong complements, then making one task extremely cheap doesn’t help that much once something else becomes the bottleneck.

Think about research. Suppose AI can write code much faster, but you still need humans to decide which experiments to run or interpret the results. You could get a substantial initial boost, but you wouldn’t necessarily get a comparable increase in the overall rate of research. That depends on whether you can substitute more of the automated work for the work that’s still constrained.

In GATE, that affects the feedback loop between AI capabilities and further AI progress. Automation can expand output and accelerate research, which can then produce better AI and more automation. Strong complementarity limits that feedback until you can automate a sufficiently broad range of tasks. Weaker complementarity allows the tasks you automate early to contribute much more to growth, even while other tasks remain unautomated.

So it’s not just a question of when AI becomes capable of doing particular things. It’s also a question of how those capabilities translate into economic output and research progress. Different assumptions about complementarity can give you quite different timelines from otherwise similar assumptions about technical progress.

r001.rationale: It explains that complementarity affects how much automating some tasks increases production while other tasks remain bottlenecks.

r002.rationale: It says automation can expand output and accelerate research, but does not state that the added output provides resources for reinvestment in AI development.

r003.rationale: It describes a feedback loop that can accelerate AI progress, but does not state that reinvesting automation-driven output gains in AI development can shorten timelines.

sol-6.1.text:
The key question is how much progress on one task helps you if you’re still bottlenecked on other tasks. Suppose AI can automate almost all the work involved in a project, but there’s a small part that still requires a human. Can you get an enormous increase in output by scaling up the automated parts, or does that remaining human task constrain the whole process? That’s what the degree of complementarity is trying to capture.

This matters especially when AI starts automating AI research. If research tasks are fairly substitutable, then automating some of them can already give you a large increase in research output. That improves AI, which lets you automate more research, and you get a feedback loop. If the tasks are highly complementary, making the automated parts faster has a smaller effect until you can also handle the bottlenecks.

So in GATE, complementarity affects how much acceleration you get from partial automation, and therefore how quickly you move toward more capable systems. It also affects the broader economic gains that can support investment in AI. You can have similar assumptions about improvements in the underlying technology and still get quite different timelines depending on how strongly those remaining tasks constrain production.

r001.rationale: It explains that complementarity determines whether automating most tasks can greatly increase output or whether the remaining human task constrains production.

r002.rationale: It says the broader economic gains from automation can support investment in AI.

r003.rationale: It links complementarity to timelines and describes a research-automation feedback loop, but does not state that reinvesting automation-driven output gains in AI development can shorten timelines.
